Rodrigo studies how ice on Earth's surface changes, mainly in Antarctica, using
satellites. Most of his work uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR): satellites
that send out radar pulses and record the echoes, so they can see the ground
through cloud and during the polar night.

## Antarctic science

Around the Antarctic coast, glaciers flow into the sea and form floating ice
tongues and ice shelves. Rodrigo's work looks at how these floating ice
features interact with the ocean and with the sea ice around them. His research
has shown that the Parker Ice Tongue broke off after the land-fast sea ice that
held it in place was lost, that ocean currents bend the Erebus Ice Tongue
sideways, and how quickly ice tongues in the western Ross Sea melt from below.

He is part of the team supervising a PhD project on how sea ice and the ice
shelf interact in McMurdo Sound, using GNSS, SAR and computer models.

## Glaciology

Rodrigo measures how fast glaciers move, how they stretch and compress, how
much ice they gain or lose, and how thick they are. He has applied these
methods in Antarctica and, with students, on glaciers in New Zealand.

## Radioglaciology

Ground-based radar can measure ice thickness and melting at the base of an ice
shelf. Rodrigo's current BIOMASS project uses ground radar instruments (ApRES
and GPR) on Antarctic ice shelves to check satellite measurements.

## Remote sensing

Rodrigo works with data from several radar satellites, including Sentinel-1,
the RADARSAT Constellation Mission, TerraSAR-X, Umbra and Capella. He uses
them to:

- measure ice movement by tracking features between images taken at different times;
- detect very small ground and ice movements by comparing the timing of radar echoes (interferometry, or InSAR);
- read surface conditions, such as wet or dry snow, from the strength of the radar echo.

He also processes airborne lidar, combines data from different sensors, uses
machine learning with satellite images, and checks results against field
measurements, including GNSS. In New Zealand he has used these methods to map
braided rivers, river-mouth lagoons (hāpua) and forest carbon.

## Current projects

- **BIOMASS calibration and validation (2025–2027):** checking data from ESA's BIOMASS satellite over Antarctic ice shelves.
- **Polarimetric radar for New Zealand glaciers (2025–2027):** using RADARSAT Constellation Mission data to track the end-of-summer snowline on glaciers in the New Zealand Alps.
- **Hāpua dynamics in Canterbury (2026):** mapping change in river-mouth lagoons with a machine learning model.
- **Penguin colonies from space (2026):** detecting penguin colonies in high-resolution SAR images.

More detail is on the [Projects](projects.qmd) page.

## Research interests

- Ice tongues, ice shelves and their interaction with the ocean
- Land-fast sea ice and sea ice
- Glacier flow, mass balance and ice thickness
- Telling short-lived surface melt apart from lasting change in the snow and firn of Antarctic ice shelves, which can come before an ice shelf breaks up
- Combining SAR, lidar and field data, including physics-guided machine learning
